TE6-F-01.hint: Sketch and label a right triangle. Decide which side is opposite, which is adjacent, and which is the hypotenuse relative to the angle in the problem. Angles of elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal.
slips: Measuring an angle of depression from the vertical instead of the horizontal.
Choosing the wrong side as the hypotenuse, such as using the ladder's height instead of its length.
Having the calculator in radian mode.

TE6-F-02.hint: Sketch the triangle. The two distances traveled are sides, and the angle between the paths is the included angle. The unknown distance is the side opposite that angle.
slips: Using the Pythagorean Theorem when the angle is not \(90\text{°}\).
Using an angle that is not between the two known sides.
Forgetting to take the square root at the end.

TE6-A-01.hint: Sketch the triangle. Find the third angle first (\(180\text{°}\) minus the other two), then use the Law of Sines with the known side, which is opposite that third angle.
slips: Matching the known side to the wrong angle. The known side is opposite the angle at the object.
Rounding an angle or a side before the final step.

parts.q: A 27-foot ladder is leaned against a wall and reaches a height of 10 feet. What angle does the ladder make with the ground? (Round to the nearest degree.)
parts.a: The ladder is the hypotenuse and the height is the side opposite the angle, so \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{10}{27}\). Then \(\theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{10}{27}\right) \approx 22\text{°}\).

parts.q: From a point 50 feet from the base of a building, the angle of elevation to its top is 50°. How tall is it? (Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.)
parts.a: The distance is the side adjacent to the angle and the height is opposite, so use the tangent: \(\tan 50\text{°} = \dfrac{h}{50}\). Then \(h = 50\tan 50\text{°} \approx 59.6\) feet.

parts.q: From the top of a 131-foot cliff, the angle of depression to a boat is 41°. How far is the boat from the base of the cliff? (Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.)

parts.q: Two boats leave the same dock on straight courses that form an angle of 30°. One boat travels 4 miles and the other boat travels 9 miles. How far apart are the boats? (Round to the nearest tenth of a mile.)
parts.a: The two paths and the line between the boats form a triangle with two known sides and the angle between them, so use the Law of Cosines: \(d^{2} = 4^{2} + 9^{2} - 2(4)(9)\cos 30\text{°}\). Then \(d \approx 5.9\) miles.

parts.q: Two observers stand 11 miles apart and both can see a boat. The angle between the line joining the observers and the line of sight to the boat is 78° at the first observer and 47° at the second observer. How far is the boat from the first observer? (Round to the nearest tenth of a mile.)
parts.a: The angle at the boat is \(C = 180\text{°} - 78\text{°} - 47\text{°} = 55\text{°}\). The side from the first observer to the boat is opposite the second observer's angle, so use the Law of Sines: \(\dfrac{d}{\sin 47\text{°}} = \dfrac{11}{\sin 55\text{°}}\). Then \(d = \dfrac{11\sin 47\text{°}}{\sin 55\text{°}} \approx 9.8\) miles.

parts.q: How far is the boat from the second observer? (Round to the nearest tenth of a mile.)
parts.a: The side from the second observer is opposite the first observer's angle: \(d = \dfrac{11\sin 78\text{°}}{\sin 55\text{°}} \approx 13.1\) miles.
